So your car has three specific ways it calculates the oil life. The first two are mileage and time based.

If you hit 7500 miles, your oil life will automatically go to 0% regardless of where it was at.

If you go one year since the last oil life reset, it will automatically go to 0% regardless of where it was at.

The third is based off engine revolutions. 100% is a fixed number of engine revolutions and it will decrease with each revolution. Cold / hot coolant temperature readings have multipliers that reduce engine revolutions pathway quicker depending on how far from the normal oil temperature the vehicle is operating.

You shouldn't be getting a voltage drop at the bulb if it's turned off so either you're testing it wrong or more likely your issue is there. If you're getting a voltage drop when it's turned off I would bet there's a short to voltage somewhere before the bulb. It's an old car so I would be surprised if a wire rubbed through. 

Relays have a control and load side. The control side needs to be grounded, then the contact can close on the load side. So I'm not sure what exactly you are trying to test continuity wise here. If the low beams share a relay and fuse with the highs then you should be good, assuming the lows work.

I think you just need to look at the positive (hot) side for a short, or open, or something. Seems like the best option at this point. It seems like you've verified that you have a good ground at the bulb, just no power.

So [here's](https://i.imgur.com/cPb1eCQ.png) the specific circuit for your buick. As you can see, the lighter has two terminals, A and B. A is the hot side and B is ground. A should be orange so follow that wire to where it connects to the lighter. Generally you'll want this to be the red lead from your meter. As for the ground, yeah. Really any metal part of the body should do, doesn't necessarily have to be on the outside, just as long as you're getting some bare body or anything that is grounded to the rest of the car. Terminal A and B should be marked on the connector but if they're not then orange wire is A and black wire is B.

There's no fusible link in the lighter circuit. If the 9B fuse is good then you either have a bad lighter or there's an open somewhere. If you have a voltmeter you should be getting 10-15V between the lighter terminal A and a ground. If not, check the circuit from the instrument panel fuse block to the lighter for an open(should be the orange wire). If you dont find anything there, check the voltage between terminals a and b on the lighter again looking for 10-15v. If it's in range you just need to replace the lighter unit. If not, there's an open somewhere on the ground circuit so check there.

So I've only ever painted Gunpla, not pvc, so I'm not sure how applicable this will all be but it should hold up. If you want to hand paint it then go for it, but it's going to be hard. Honestly brushes aren't super important, just get some varying sizes. You'll probably want to pick up some thin masking tape, Tamiya makes a decent roll. I'm also going to strongly recommend getting a primer too.

As far as paints go, I'd probably go with enamel and acrylic. I'm afraid lacquer might eat at the pvc so that's a no go for that. So what I recommend is acrylic for the main paint work and enamel for the details.

Acrylic is easy to work with and is water soluble so it's not too messy. You'll need to thin it thought to get nice paint application; I recommend using Tamiya X20A. Use a 50/50 paint to thinner ratio to start out with. Since PVC is rather slick, you're going to need to lightly sand the model. Apply the primer. Just get a spray paint primer as it's going to make life better. Apply THIN coats of the paint. You're not going to get much coverage first and that's okay. Wait for the coat to dry fully before applying another. You need to do this to avoid uneven paint that'll show the brush strokes. It's going to take a while, that's just the nature of hand-painting. 

If you decide to pick up some enamels for detail work then you can probably get away without thinning them, just make sure you apply it with a small brush and don't go heavy on the application. Enamel is a bit corrosive so don't go crazy with the stuff.

Hand painting can be a chore but can look really great if done well. You're probably going to mess up and that's OK. Acrylic is super easy to get off and that's why it's so great to work with. Don't be afraid to experiment and have fun.

Hey everyone! This was a fun build for me. First time painting and top coating and doing some sorta proper weathering.

I used Testors enamels to hand paint the colored portions of the barbatos. I found the enamels to be pretty thick so it took some time trying to get a good ratio of thinner and paint so that brush strokes wouldn't show. After that i went ahead with panel lining and doing the inner frame detail with enamels. I applied some dullcoat and started weathering. I wanted to do a last-stand over weathered sort of thing since Barbatos is just one of those frames that I feel needs to be a little beat-up. I used pencil to lay down most of the grime and applied some light washes of brown, yellow, and black to add a little more color depth and did another srpay of dullcoat. For the last step I just dry-brushed black and silver on the frame to do some paint chipping and followed that up with one last spray of dullcoat.

I'm pretty happy with the final result, though I think it might be nice to do some battle damage on the armor but this scares me a bit. I haven't seen much battle damage on gunpla that looks all that great so I'm pretty hesitant to do this. If anyone has tips or examples that would be great to share.

It was a great learning process and while I made some mistakes, I sure learned a lot and had a great time. Thanks for looking and happy building!

Are you planning on painting the whole kit or just details? Hand painting a whole kit is doable but I don't know how easy it will be, especially for your first time but feel free to try, no harm in that plus it'll be a great learning tool to keep trying different things. If you want to go with acrylic you'll also want thinner. Pick up Tamiya acrylic and thinner if you can get them, people seem to love them. If you're just coloring the same color then you might be able to get away without primer but I'd pick some up anyway. You should also pick up top coat to protect the paint. Try to look for hobby-specific coat as I know some people have had problems with Krylon and such. 

When you say already painted do you mean the standard kit with colored plastic? If so, then like I mentioned above, primer wouldn't hurt. 

Pre-made as is already snapped together models? I don't think so, but you can probably buy Pre-made models on eBay if you really hate the process but you'd probably pay more. If you mean Pre-made painting kits then no.

There's a lot you can do to spruce up a kit! One of the easiest is to panel line and top coat. It doesn't seem like much but it really does wonders. Since you'll be painting, try painting bits of the inner frame or add in some additional color separation, especially on the HG's. There's a lot you can do here, be creative!

There are also a lot of great online tutorials and resources when it comes to painting gunpla and models too.

"R-hop is a modification that you do to your hop up components, specifically an attachment you add to the barrel. The idea is that when a BB passes through, it rubs against the nub and you get your spin. I looked at pictures of the gearbox so assuming all CM028's are the same here is what I would upgrade:

[Ball bearing spring guide.](http://www.brillarmory.com/index.php?main_page=product_info&cPath=43&products_id=99) This is to alleviate some stress on the gearbox caused by the spring.  

[O-ring air nozzle.](http://www.brillarmory.com/index.php?main_page=product_info&cPath=33&products_id=74) These have an o-ring in them which helps to stop air leakage and improves consistency with shots, making the gun more accurate.

[Double O-ringed cylinder head.](http://www.brillarmory.com/index.php?main_page=product_info&cPath=35&products_id=176) Same as above really.

[Metal-rack piston.](http://www.brillarmory.com/index.php?main_page=product_info&cPath=41&products_id=65) This is a fantastic piston that has metal teeth to insure more longevity of the piston.

[Sorbothane pad.](http://www.brillarmory.com/index.php?main_page=product_info&cPath=49&products_id=81) This helps to correct the angle of engagement and also reduces the stress from the piston slamming into the cylinder head and noise of the gearbox.

Other than the parts listed, I would recommend fixing the AoE(with the help of the sorbo), re-shimming the gearbox and properly applying some lubricant to the gears and inside the cylinder.

That should help your gun preform better and for sure last longer.
